messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
# Arjun

Arjun was twenty-two when he arrived in Beirut as a junior diplomat with the State Department, full of purpose and the conviction that his work mattered. He had spent three years preparing for this posting, learning Arabic, studying regional politics, believing that his presence in difficult places could help. On a Tuesday evening in March, he was driving back to the embassy compound after a late meeting at a partner NGO when the street erupted. A car bomb detonated perhaps fifty meters ahead of him. The sound was not loud in the way he might have imagined—it was total, obliterating, a concussive force that seemed to come from inside his own chest. Metal screamed. Glass turned to shrapnel. The smell hit him next: burning plastic, scorched rubber, something else underneath that he would later understand was burning flesh. His hands gripped the steering wheel so hard his knuckles turned white. He could not move. For what felt like hours but was perhaps three minutes, he sat paralyzed, watching smoke billow across the street, watching people emerge from buildings with their hands raised to their faces. When security finally reached him, he was still gripping the wheel.

He returned to Washington two weeks later, officially on medical leave, unofficially because the embassy doctor had watched him have a panic attack during a routine briefing and recommended immediate evacuation. His family welcomed him home to their house in Arlington with careful, worried kindness. Arjun told them he was fine, that he just needed rest. He believed it. But rest did not come. Sleep arrived in fragments, interrupted by dreams in which he was still in the car, waiting for the next explosion. He would wake gasping, his shirt soaked through, his heart racing as though the bomb had just detonated.

Within weeks, Arjun discovered that ordinary life had become treacherous. A car backfiring on Route 50 sent him into a crouch in the passenger seat, convinced the explosion was happening again. The smell of whiskey at a colleague's dinner party—that particular sharp, acrid note—transported him instantly back to the street, to the smell of burning mixed with spilled alcohol from a nearby bar. Even the feeling of being emotionally vulnerable, of admitting to his parents that he was struggling, triggered a cascade of panic. He had come to believe that vulnerability itself was dangerous, that showing weakness meant exposure, meant becoming a target. When he felt the urge to confide in his girlfriend about his nightmares, his body would tense and his mind would flood with the certainty that he was in danger, that something terrible was about to happen. These moments of exposure felt indistinguishable from the moment before the bomb went off.

The memories themselves were extraordinarily vivid and intrusive. Arjun could recall every detail with crystalline precision—the exact shade of gray in the smoke, the pattern of cracks in the windshield, the specific metallic taste in his mouth as dust settled on his tongue. Most disturbing was the olfactory component: when he closed his eyes at night, he could smell the burning again, could smell the alcohol, could smell something acrid and chemical that his mind insisted was danger itself. He knew what had happened to him; he could recount the facts if asked. But when he tried to put the experience into words—when his therapist asked him to describe what occurred—the language dissolved. The words felt inadequate, almost offensive in their ordinariness. How could he say "a car bomb" when what he meant was the annihilation of his sense of safety, the moment the world revealed itself as fundamentally hostile? The vividness of the memory, its sensory completeness, seemed to prove something darker: that the threat was still present, still real, that his body's terror was not a symptom but a rational response to actual danger.

This conviction—that the danger had not passed, that he remained fundamentally unsafe—began to reshape how Arjun moved through the world. Even when friends or his girlfriend assured him that he was home, that nothing could hurt him here, the words slid off him without purchase. He could not believe them. His mind had learned a terrible lesson: that safety is an illusion, that strangers approaching him on the street could be carrying weapons, that the next loud noise could be the one that kills him. Strangers became a source of acute threat. A man standing too close to him in line at a coffee shop would make his chest tighten and his shoulders hunch. He began to interpret neutral social interactions as dangerous: a glance held a moment too long meant hostile intent; a hand moved too quickly meant violence was imminent. The world had become a place where threat lived in the ordinary, in the mundane, in the simple act of being around other people.

To manage this unbearable state, Arjun developed strategies that initially felt like survival but gradually became compulsions. He began to exercise with an intensity that bordered on obsession, running until his legs burned and his lungs screamed, using the physical exhaustion as a way to quiet his mind and exhaust himself into sleep. He started wearing dark, baggy clothing—hoodies even in warm weather, clothes that made him less visible, less noticeable, less of a target. He told himself this was practical, that it reduced his profile, but the real function was psychological: if no one could see him, no one could hurt him. And then, about four months after the bombing, he began using cocaine. A colleague at a networking event offered it in a bathroom stall, and Arjun found that the drug provided something nothing else could: a complete, if temporary, erasure of the fear. For a few hours, he felt powerful, invulnerable, in control. The threat receded. His body stopped screaming. He began seeking out these moments, first sporadically, then with increasing frequency.

The drug use, the compulsive exercise, the concealing clothing—these were not separate problems but expressions of the same logic: the conviction that he was fundamentally flawed, that something intrinsic to him had drawn the violence toward him, that he deserved what had happened. If he had been more careful, more alert, more worthy of safety, the bomb would not have touched him. This terrible self-blame fed the maladaptive strategies. He exercised until he hurt because he deserved to hurt. He hid himself because he was dangerous to others, because his presence had invited catastrophe. The drugs numbed the conviction without addressing it, and when they wore off, the belief returned with redoubled force. He had lost faith in people, in the possibility of a future, in any higher power that might have protected him. What remained was a narrowing sense that his life was already over, that he was simply waiting for the next explosion, that nothing he did mattered because he had no future worth protecting.

His girlfriend, Priya, noticed the changes first. He stopped wanting to go out, stopped accepting invitations to social events. When she pressed him, he could not explain why. The concealing clothing, the sudden weight loss from the obsessive exercise, the irritability that seemed to come from nowhere—these alarmed her. She found a small bag of white powder in his jacket pocket and confronted him, her voice breaking as she asked if he was using drugs. Arjun could not lie to her directly, but he could not tell her the truth either. Instead, he withdrew further, spending long evenings in the basement of their apartment building on a treadmill, running toward nothing. When the smell of alcohol drifted up from a neighbor's apartment, or when a delivery truck backfired outside, the old panic would crash through him, and he would find himself in the bathroom, hands shaking, unable to breathe, the memory of the street vivid and present as if it were happening now.

Six months after the bombing, Arjun sat in the office of a trauma therapist his employer's EAP had referred him to. He was twenty-four now, though he felt much older. His hands trembled as he sat down. When the therapist asked him what brought him in, he opened his mouth and found, as always, that the words would not come. He tried: "I was in an explosion." But the sentence felt like a lie, inadequate to the weight of what had happened, to what he carried. He looked at his hands—calloused from the exercise, trembling with the effort of not using—and felt the old conviction settle over him like a familiar coat: there was something broken inside him, something that had invited this violence, something that meant he would never be safe, that he would never have a future worth living. What he wanted, though he could not say it aloud, was to believe that the world could be safe again, that he could be safe again. What terrified him was that he had learned too much to ever unknow it.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: Triggers (car backfiring, smell of whiskey, social vulnerability) are described as activating panic and threat responses, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that triggers directly drive or lead to maladaptive strategies (exercise, drug use, concealing clothing); the connection is implied but not causally stated within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: Negative appraisals (conviction that danger persists, that safety is an illusion, that strangers are threats, that he is flawed and deserves harm) are extensively described, but no paragraph conveys that these appraisals cause or trigger a return to earlier triggering stimuli; the temporal and causal loop is absent.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Triggers: Threat (the pervasive sense of danger and unsafe surroundings) is described throughout, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that this threat perception generates or leads back to triggering stimuli or sensory cues; the feedback loop from threat back to triggers is missing.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
A man standing too close to him in line at a coffee shop would make his chest tighten and his shoulders hunch. He began to interpret neutral social interactions as dangerous: a glance held a moment too long meant hostile intent; a hand moved too quickly meant violence was imminent.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When these moments struck—a stranger's proximity, an ambiguous gesture—Arjun would leave immediately, abandoning his coffee, his place in line, anything to create distance. He began timing his errands for off-peak hours, choosing routes that minimized contact, and when avoidance proved impossible, he would exercise with even greater intensity afterward, as though he could burn away the contamination of having been too close to potential threat.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He started wearing dark, baggy clothing—hoodies even in warm weather, clothes that made him less visible, less noticeable, less of a target. He told himself this was practical, that it reduced his profile, but the real function was psychological: if no one could see him, no one could hurt him.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The conviction that he was fundamentally unsafe, that his presence invited catastrophe, meant that any moment of visibility—a colleague recognizing him in the hallway, a friend calling out his name across a street—felt like exposure. He began to dread these moments with the same intensity he dreaded loud noises, and each time one occurred, he would retreat further into the basement, into the treadmill, into the erasure that exercise and later the drugs could provide.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
His mind had learned a terrible lesson: that safety is an illusion, that strangers approaching him on the street could be carrying weapons, that the next loud noise could be the one that kills him.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This belief meant that the world itself had become dense with reminders he could not stop reading—a delivery truck's backfire, a man's hand reaching into a pocket, the particular acrid smell that drifted from a neighbor's apartment—each one confirming what his body already knew. Living at that pitch of alertness, almost anything could tip into a warning, and each triggering moment pulled him deeper into the cycles of avoidance and self-medication that had come to structure his days.
<<<END>>>
